Troubler
TRUB-lur
n. (one who brings calamity on a people; Ahab's accusation against Elijah)
From Latin turbulare, to disturb, from turba, a crowd or tumult, through Old French troubler. In 1 Kings it renders Hebrew akar, to stir up muddy water, and so to bring ruin — the root behind the valley of Achor.

Biblical Definition

Three years of drought, and when Ahab finally meets the prophet who announced it he opens with an accusation: Art thou he that troubleth Israel? Elijah's answer is one of the great refusals in Scripture, and it does not hedge. I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the LORD, and thou hast followed Baalim. The man who announced the drought is not the man who caused it. Hebrew akar means to stir up water until it is undrinkable, and it names the valley where Achan was stoned — Joshua said to him, Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day, and the place was called Achor after it. So the word carries a settled meaning: the troubler of a people is the one whose sin brings judgment on the whole, not the one who names it. Paul uses it the same way of men unsettling the Galatian churches — there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ — and the troublers there are the ones adding to the gospel, not Paul who was resisting them. The accusation always runs the same direction, and so does the truth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who troubles or disturbs; one who afflicts or molests; a disturber of peace or order.

expand to see more

TROUBLER, n. One who troubles or disturbs; one who afflicts or molests; a disturber.

TROUBLE, v.t. To agitate; to disturb; to put into confused motion.

TROUBLE, v.t. To afflict; to grieve; to distress; to perplex.

DISTURB, v.t. To stir; to move; to discompose; to excite from a state of rest or tranquillity.

PERVERT, v.t. To turn from truth, propriety, or from its proper purpose; to distort from its true use or end.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 18:17 — "And it came to pass, when Ahab saw Elijah, that Ahab said unto him, Art thou he that troubleth Israel?"

1 Kings 18:18 — "And he answered, I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the LORD, and thou hast followed Baalim."

Joshua 7:25 — "And Joshua said, Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him with stones, and burned them with fire, after they had stoned them with stones."

Galatians 1:7 — "Which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ."

Modern Corruption

The one who names a sin is treated as the cause of the trouble it brings; Elijah answers the charge by naming who actually forsook the commandments, and Scripture keeps the word for those whose sin brings the judgment.

expand to see more

Ahab's move is perfectly modern: locate the disturbance in the person who mentioned the problem. It is effective because it is partly true — things were calm before Elijah came, and they were not calm afterward. Every church that has ever disciplined a member, every man who has told a friend the truth about his life, has met the same accounting. Elijah's reply is worth memorizing for its structure as much as its courage: he denies the charge flatly, then states the actual cause, then names the responsible party to his face. He does not apologize for the drought, and he does not pretend it was pleasant.

The word must not be turned into a licence for quarrelsomeness, because Scripture also knows real troublers inside the church. The Galatian troublers were not plain speakers; they were men adding requirements to the gospel and unsettling young believers, and Paul says let them be accursed. Proverbs says a froward man soweth strife, and that he that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind. The test is not whether a man causes disturbance but what he is disturbing it over: Elijah over the commandments of the LORD forsaken, Paul over the gospel of Christ perverted. Trouble raised over anything less is just trouble.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew akar (H5916), to stir up, to trouble, to bring ruin; Akor (H5911), Achor; Greek tarasso (G5015), to agitate; metastrepho (G3344), to pervert.

expand to see more

Hebrew akar (H5916) — to stir water into mud; used of Achan, of Elijah's accusers, and of Jephthah's daughter.

Hebrew Akor (H5911) — Achor, trouble; the valley named for Achan, and promised as a door of hope in Hosea.

Greek tarasso (G5015) — to agitate, to trouble; used of the Galatian troublers and of the Lord's own soul.

Greek metastrepho (G3344) — to turn about, to pervert; what the troublers were doing to the gospel.

Hebrew Baalim (H1168) — the Baals; what Elijah names as the true cause of the drought.

Usage

"“Art thou he that troubleth Israel?” — the accusation aimed at the messenger."

"“I have not troubled Israel; but thou” — the charge returned with the evidence."

"“there be some that trouble you” — the word used of real troublers in a church."
